questions.question: What extra steps must an NBFC take before opening an account for a politically exposed person?
questions.answer: Besides normal customer due diligence, an NBFC that opens an account for a PEP must have risk management systems to determine whether the customer or beneficial owner is a PEP, take reasonable measures to establish the source of funds or wealth, and get senior management approval to open the account. It must also subject the account to enhanced ongoing monitoring. If an existing customer later becomes a PEP, it needs senior management approval to continue the relationship. These steps also apply to family members and close associates of PEPs.

questions.question: How must an NBFC carry out the digital KYC process?
questions.answer: Based on the passages provided, an NBFC must build its own digital KYC application, make it available at customer touch points, and do KYC only through that application. It must control access so that only authorised officials can use it, through a login-id and password or a Live OTP or Time OTP mechanism. The customer and the authorised official meet in person, and the customer holds the original OVD. The official takes a live photograph of the customer and embeds it in the Customer Application Form (CAF). The application must watermark the photo with the CAF number, GPS coordinates, official's name, employee code, date and time. It must capture only a live photograph, against a white background with no other person in the frame. After successful verification, the authorised officer digitally signs the CAF, prints it, and gets the customer's signature or thumb impression. The officer then scans and uploads it, and the original hard copy may be returned to the customer. questions.question: What is the cooling-off period for digital loans?
questions.answer: There is no single fixed cooling-off period. Each NBFC sets it in its credit policy, but it cannot be shorter than one day. During this period the borrower must be given an explicit option to exit a digital loan by paying the principal and the proportionate APR, without any penalty. The NBFC may keep a reasonable one-time processing fee if the borrower exits during this period, and it must disclose that fee upfront in the KFS.

questions.question: Who handles complaints about digital lending, and what must the lender do about them?
questions.answer: The NBFC and any of its LSPs that interface with the borrower must designate nodal grievance redressal officers to handle digital lending complaints. Their contact details must be prominently displayed on the websites of the NBFC and the LSP, on the DLA, and in the KFS. The facility to lodge complaints must also be available on the DLA and those websites, and responsibility for grievance redressal stays with the NBFC. If the NBFC rejects a complaint wholly or partly, the borrower is not satisfied with the reply, or no reply comes within 30 days, the borrower can complain through the RBI's CMS portal under the Integrated Ombudsman Scheme or send a physical complaint to the RBI's Centralised Receipt and Processing Centre in Chandigarh. The NBFC must suitably convey this information to the borrower. The NBFC's own website must also show its customer care and internal grievance redressal details and a link to the RBI's CMS and Sachet Portal.

questions.question: What does para 18 of the Credit Facilities Directions require?
questions.answer: Para 18 of the Credit Facilities Directions deals with reporting of digital lending apps (DLAs) to the RBI. An NBFC must report all DLAs it deploys or joins, whether its own or those of lending service providers (LSPs), on the RBI's CIMS portal in the prescribed format. It must update the list when DLAs are added or engagements end. The Chief Compliance Officer or a Board-designated official must certify that the data is correct and that the DLAs comply with the extant regulatory instructions. That official must also certify specific aspects, such as the DLA's link to the NBFC's website, a nodal grievance officer for LSP-owned DLAs, compliant data collection and storage, and website disclosure of DLA particulars. The NBFC must ensure the data is correct and timely, because the RBI publishes it without verifying it, and it must deal with customer grievances about DLAs directly. It must also ensure that listing a third-party DLA is not presented as RBI registration, authorization or endorsement.

questions.question: What must a notice from a Data Fiduciary to a Data Principal contain?
questions.answer: The notice must be presented and understandable independently of other information from the Data Fiduciary. It must give, in clear and plain language, a fair account of the details needed for specific and informed consent, including at least an itemised description of the personal data and the specified purposes, with a specific description of the goods, services or uses enabled by the processing. It must also give the communication link to the Data Fiduciary's website or app, and describe other means, if any, to withdraw consent (as easily as it was given), exercise rights under the Act, and complain to the Board.

questions.question: What security safeguards must a Data Fiduciary put in place to protect personal data?
questions.answer: A Data Fiduciary must take reasonable security safeguards to prevent personal data breach, covering processing by its Data Processors too. At a minimum these include: data security measures such as encryption, obfuscation, masking or virtual tokens; controls on access to computer resources; logs, monitoring and review to detect unauthorised access, investigate and remediate it; measures for continued processing if data is compromised, such as backups; retaining such logs and personal data for one year unless another law requires otherwise; contract provisions with Data Processors requiring reasonable security safeguards; and appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure the safeguards are effectively observed.

questions.question: When is a purpose deemed no longer served, so that personal data must be erased?
questions.answer: Under Rule 8, for a Data Fiduciary of a class and purpose listed in the Third Schedule, the purpose is treated as no longer served when the Data Principal neither approaches it for the specified purpose nor exercises her rights for the time period specified in the Third Schedule. The data must then be erased, unless retention is needed to comply with a law. At least 48 hours before the period ends, the Data Fiduciary must tell the Data Principal that the data will be erased unless she logs in or otherwise makes contact. Separately, personal data and logs must be kept for at least one year from processing before erasure, unless another law or the Government requires longer retention.

questions.question: How must a Data Fiduciary get consent before processing a child's personal data?
questions.answer: Before processing any personal data of a child, a Data Fiduciary must adopt appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure verifiable consent of the parent is obtained. It must also exercise due diligence to check that the person claiming to be the parent is an identifiable adult. This check uses either reliable identity and age details the Data Fiduciary already holds, or identity and age details voluntarily provided by the individual or through a virtual token issued by an authorised entity. An adult is someone who has completed eighteen years. Where the parent is not a registered user, the check is made against details issued by an entity entrusted by law or the Government, or a virtual token mapped to them, and the parent may provide these via a Digital Locker service provider.

questions.question: Can an NBFC add penal interest to my loan's interest rate when I miss a payment?
questions.answer: No. For loans covered by these rules, an NBFC cannot add penal interest to the interest rate when a borrower defaults or misses a payment. Any penalty must be charged as 'penal charges', which must be reasonable, applied only on the amount in default, and not capitalised. The NBFC may still charge interest on unpaid interest, including unpaid EMI, at the contracted rate until the default is remedied, but not at a penal rate. These rules apply to fresh loans from April 1, 2024, and to existing loans from June 30, 2024, and they exclude credit cards, external commercial borrowings, trade credits, structured obligations and other foreign currency loans.
